title: Short Stuff: Great Smog of London
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Great Smog of London, December 1952, when coal smoke combined with fog over five days (December 5 to 9) under a stagnant high-pressure system, causing mass deaths and shutdowns. The hosts cover how transport and daily life were disrupted, estimates of deaths (about 4,000 historically, possibly 12,000 by current estimates), and the Clean Air Act of 1956 and later measures. The episode also includes off-topic banter about Chuck's daughter, Jeopardy, and Peter McNerney.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the Great Smog
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the Short Stuff episode, noting the earlier London stink and smog episodes, and introduce the Great Smog of December 1952 as smoke plus fog that London named the Great Smog.

segments.title: How the smog formed and its early effects
segments.summary: The hosts explain that London's smog history went back to the thirteenth century and that the term smog was coined by a Londoner. Factory, household chimney, and vehicle smoke combined with fog in December, shutting down driving, Thames shipping, and bus service, while the Underground stayed usable.

segments.title: Indoor conditions and reported hazards
segments.summary: The hosts describe reports of cinemas unable to show films, people unable to see their feet, and a claim, which Chuck says he could not confirm, that people walked into the Thames and drowned. Crime and purse snatching are also discussed as likely increases.

segments.title: Off-topic banter and sponsor-style break
segments.summary: Hosts chat about Chuck's daughter's interest in Jeopardy and Story Pirates, and a family visit with Peter McNerney, before a break.

segments.title: Why the smog lasted five days and death toll
segments.summary: The hosts say the smog lasted five days, December 5 to 9, because a high-pressure anticyclone about thirty miles wide trapped smoke near ground level. Estimated deaths were about 4,000 at the time and may be closer to 12,000 by current estimates, with the caveat that some victims already had respiratory conditions. A herd of cattle in Smithfield is also said to have died.

segments.title: Policy response: Clean Air Act and later measures
segments.summary: The British government responded with the Clean Air Act in 1956. The hosts say a later smog crisis in 1962 led to stronger measures, including incentives, industry restrictions, and a shift from coal to electricity, natural gas, or oil. They say there has not been a great smog since 1962, and compare to Los Angeles smog.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up, saying they want to return to London for live shows, thank listeners, and credit the episode idea to a producer.
